look_here_first: GIANT REED: Look for tall, thick, jointed canes with broad leaves that wrap around the stem. A mature plant has a large branching flower plume at the top. Start with the whole plant, then check the leaf collar and flowering parts to rule out common reed (Phragmites).

best_field_traits: Start with a very tall stand of thick, jointed, cane-like stems.
Look for long, broad leaves whose bases wrap around the stem.
Find the large, many-branched plume at the tip of a mature cane.
For closer confirmation, inspect the real leaf collar and one mature multi-flowered spikelet.
Tall cane-like culms, commonly 2–6 m in the existing Kew-based review.
Thick rhizomes and broad flat leaves.
Large feathery terminal panicle, to about 70 cm; spikelets around 1 cm in the existing review.
morphology_keys.habit: Dense stands of tall cane-like stems; selected photograph shows a stand in Maui, not a Texas locality.
morphology_keys.leaves: Broad flat grass blades on conspicuous culms; sheath and ligule require close photographs.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Large terminal panicle; panicle architecture and spikelet detail remain photo gaps.
morphology_keys.lookalike_separators: ARUNDO vs PHRAGMITES: Both make tall jointed riparian canes and feathery heads. Arundo usually has broad clasping leaf bases, a robust cane and a more upright branching panicle; common reed often has a more drooping plume. A definitive flowering check is WHERE HAIRS GROW: Arundo has a glabrous RACHILLA (axis between florets) but silky hairs on the basal lemma/callus; Phragmites has LONG SILKY RACHILLA HAIRS and usually glabrous lemmas. Their ligules can BOTH be fringed — a 'hairless Arundo ligule' is NOT a dependable rule. Do not call a Phragmites stand introduced/invasive without independent lineage evidence.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: GIANT REED: begin with robust jointed canes and broad clasping leaves; inspect the actual leaf collar and mature flowering plume in the licensed macro panels. For look-alike Phragmites, confirm glabrous Arundo spikelet RACHILLA versus long silky Phragmites rachilla hairs on a magnified ripe spikelet; the Arundo ligule itself CAN have a ciliate fringe. No removal or exact Phragmites lineage ID from plume size alone.
crew_checkpoints: FIRST: view archived whole stand—dense robust cane-like culms and broad drooping leaves suggest giant reed but do not identify it alone.

SECOND: use the photographed true blade/sheath junction. A pale rounded clasping base and ciliate membranous ligule are visible. Both Arundo and Phragmites can have a fringed ligule; hair presence at collar is NOT a safe binary split.
THIRD: see the branching terminal Arundo flowering plume in the new source photo; it tends more upright, but panicle shape varies and is not conclusive.

FOURTH (DECISIVE WITH A MICROSCOPE): remove one ripe spikelet with permission, open it over a millimeter scale. Arundo: rachilla itself hairless; white hairs on lower lemma/callus. Phragmites: long silky hairs ON the rachilla between florets, typically glabrous lemma.

FIFTH: do NOT confuse species ID with nativity. Arundo donax is introduced in Texas; Phragmites australis includes native North American, introduced Eurasian and southern Gulf Coast lineages. Resolve any Phragmites lineage separately before treatment.

look_alikes.check: Use mature SAME-SPECIMEN spikelets: Phragmites rachilla with long silky hairs versus Arundo rachilla glabrous, hairs chiefly on Arundo lemma/callus. Both can have ciliate ligules. Native lineage/introduced provenance remains a separate management decision.

Native giant cutgrass can form tall waterside stands; compare its more open grass panicle, extremely rough cutting leaf margins, and very different floret/spikelet arrangement. Do not classify from height or proximity to water alone.
Tall introduced Johnsongrass with characteristic conspicuously paired spikelets on an open branched panicle rather than the true Arundo floret group; generally narrower leaves and smaller canes.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: GIANT REED: follow one robust 2–6 m jointed cane to broad leaves with rounded clasping blade-base lobes and a dense 30–60 cm plume. At the true collar find a short CILIATE MEMBRANOUS ligule. Do not separate from Phragmites by plume size or ligule hairs alone: inspect a ripe floret for where the silky hairs originate.

measurable_field_key.growth_form: Robust rhizomatous perennial, erect cane-like culms commonly 2–6 m; thick knotty woody rhizomes and many jointed culms, not an annual tuft. Leaf blades commonly 30–60 cm by 2.5–5 cm, rounded to clasping at base.
measurable_field_key.ligule_collar: Short membranous ligule with ciliate fringe, reported 0.7–2 mm in regional floras; rounded/ear-like clasping blade-base lobes; do not mistake adjacent sheath-mouth hairs for the membrane. Measure a true opened blade–sheath junction with 1-mm scale.
measurable_field_key.panicle: Large, profusely branched, often upright oblong plume, commonly 30–60 cm long; shape is supportive, not diagnostic against common reed.
measurable_field_key.spikelet: Pedicelled laterally compressed spikelets approximately 8–15 mm, commonly 3–5 florets; florets disarticulate above persistent glumes. Do not call a whole spikelet one seed.
measurable_field_key.glumes: Two persistent, roughly equal narrow membranous glumes, often 8.5–13 mm, each typically 3–5-veined, mostly glabrous and without long awns. Published ranges vary; use attached mature material and a millimeter rule.
measurable_field_key.lemma_palea: Fertile lemma generally 6–12 mm, 3–9-veined depending regional treatment, conspicuously silky-hairy on its lower back/callus with hairs often 5–8 mm. Palea shorter, usually about half to two-thirds lemma length, two-veined and ciliate on keels.
measurable_field_key.awn: Glumes essentially awnless. Fertile lemma apex may be minutely two-toothed and bear a SHORT median awn/awnlet, approximately 1–3 mm, arising near/between apical teeth; do not mislabel the long silky lemma hairs as awns.
measurable_field_key.decisive_hair_placement: Between successive florets, the Arundo rachilla internodes are glabrous or lack the conspicuous long silky rachilla hairs of Phragmites; Arundo silk is chiefly on lemma backs and floret bases. A basal tuft near the lowest floret may occur, so never oversimplify to 'every part of rachilla hairless'.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.local_lookalikes: Phragmites australis: rhizomatous wetland reed with long silky hairs along the rachilla between florets and usually glabrous lemmas; native, introduced and Gulf Coast lineages require independent evidence. Zizaniopsis miliacea: native giant cutgrass, extremely rough cutting leaf margins and different male/female floral organization; do not decide from stand height. Sorghum halepense: tall rhizomatous Johnsongrass with paired sessile/pedicellate spikelets in an open panicle rather than Arundo's multi-flowered spikelets.
last_mile_photo_arrow_gaps: SAME TEXAS PLANT: rooted or previously disturbed rhizome, intact jointed culm node, broad clasping leaf base and complete plume with centimeter ruler; no new excavation solely for a photograph.
TRUE COLLAR 10–20×: opened blade–sheath junction with short fringed membrane and clasping lobes, measured against 1-mm scale; compare Phragmites collar at matching scale.
MATURE SPIKELET 10–20×: intact 8–15 mm spikelet, two detached glumes with veins, and individual fertile lemma/palea; each with 1-mm ruler and independent specimen determination.

DECISIVE DISSECTION: same specimen Arundo rachilla internodes versus basal lemma/callus hairs, paired with verified Phragmites rachilla hairs at same magnification. Arrow only anatomically visible structures.
AWN DETAIL: isolated fertile lemma apex with short 1–3 mm median awnlet, distinguish from 5–8 mm basal silk and glume tips; photo-rights and attribution verified individually.

Recognize the large rhizomatous reed, but do not claim any ONE photo proves root-to-head linkage or Texas provenance. A permitted disturbed Texas specimen with roots/canes/head in one documented series remains desirable.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Rounded clasping blade base; a short ciliate membranous ligule, approximately 0.7–2 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The Harry Rose Australian CC BY 2.0 macro (panel 3) genuinely shows a wide rounded clasping leaf base and a short membranous ligula-like flange with pale marginal hairs. Existing arrows mark the blade, clasping lobes and white hairs only. A physical 1-mm ruler and Texas voucher would let us measure its 0.7–2 mm literature ligule range, but the actual collar photograph does not include a reliable millimeter ruler. Phragmites can also have a ciliate membranous ligule; do not separate these reeds solely by visible fringe.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE SPECIES COLLAR PHOTO PRESENT — 1-MM LOCAL SCALE AND PHRAGMITES MATCH MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE ONE MATURE SPIKELET AND ITS GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Spikelets about 8–15 mm with multiple florets; two persistent 3–5-veined glumes usually about 8–13 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open a mature attached spikelet under 10–20× and separate the TWO basal glumes from the several individual florets. Count glume veins and measure each part; do not call the entire multi-flowered spikelet one seed. These measurements are published botanical ranges, not dimensions established from the archived photos.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LITERATURE MEASUREMENTS — DISSECTION AND SCALE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA SILK IS NOT A LONG AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile lemma roughly 6–12 mm; basal/back hairs 5–8 mm; short median awnlet usually 1–3 mm where present.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Locate the hairy fertile lemma and its callus, then examine the apex for a short median awnlet between tiny teeth. The silky basal hairs are NOT awns. Most importantly, examine the rachilla between successive florets: Arundo lacks the long conspicuous silky rachilla hairs characteristic of Phragmites. The basal floret region can bear hair tufts, so do not oversimplify to 'every axis hairless'.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS REED LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Phragmites: long silky rachilla hairs; giant cutgrass: different floral structure; Johnsongrass: paired sorghum spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Confirm the hair origin in a mature Arundo/Phragmites spikelet pair, not merely a drooping plume or ciliate collar. Native giant cutgrass (Zizaniopsis miliacea) has cutting leaf margins and distinct reproductive units. Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) has sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs. Native versus introduced Phragmites lineage is a separate determination and must not be inferred from reed appearance.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TEXT COMPARISON READY — MATCHED TEXAS MACROS NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — real rhizome reference, not a connected Texas voucher
field_id_short_tiles.details: CURRENT ROLE COVERAGE: FOUR original local photos (2 stand/growth views, true collar, complete attached plume), ONE newly linked JMK real photographed heavy woody RHIZOME under CC BY-SA 4.0; the rhizome remains external and not same-plant linked to a head. Keep the original introduced/non-native status. No new JPEG bytes in repository and no new gross arrows.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Giant reed: whole cane → leaf base → flowering head → spikelet
steps: 1 · Spot the giant cane: thick jointed stems and broad leaves make a tall, often dense patch (whole-plant photos above).
2 · Find the collar where a leaf meets the stem. Notice the rounded clasping leaf-base shoulders and pale hairy-edged ligule (see arrows).
3 · Look at the large branching flowering plume. Each narrow branch carries spikelets; this head alone cannot rule out Phragmites.
4 · When flowering, zoom in on a mature spikelet. Learn which scales are glumes and which parts are florets; the hair-attachment difference from Phragmites needs close magnification.
5 · If the leaf junction or reproductive details are missing, keep the ID tentative and compare common reed.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The photos teach giant reed, but the exact microscopic origin of silky spikelet hairs still needs a matched close-up. Do not identify Phragmites lineage or make removal decisions from plume size alone.
advanced_steps_preserved_20261027: 1 · RHIZOME PHOTO — panel 2 is an actual source-labelled external JMK CC BY-SA 4.0 Arundo rhizome from South Africa, NOT a new archived Texas photo. See thick woody ringed horizontal internodes and old CUT ROUND CANE BASES; don't call these cut bases roots.

3 · TRUE INNER COLLAR — Harry Rose's locally archived panel 3 clearly shows the clasping leaf-base shoulders and actual pale fringed ligule; its three arrows label broad visible parts, not mm length. Distinguish side hairs from the free membranous rim.

These are true Arundo, not Phragmites. The exact origin of microscopic silk on lemma vs rachilla is still pending verified close-up; no invented arrows.

beginner_learning_path.title: Giant reed — learn it in four photographs
beginner_learning_path.intro: Start with a whole plant. Then inspect the leaf base and flower head. The last picture shows the reproductive parts that help distinguish this grass from common reed.
beginner_learning_path.memory_rule: Thick jointed canes → broad clasping leaves → upright branching plume → check the spikelet.

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the whole plant
steps.look_for: See the tall stand of stout, jointed, upright canes with wide green leaves. This tells you what giant reed looks like from several steps away.
steps.why_it_matters: This is your first clue, not proof: common reed and giant cutgrass can also form tall stands.

steps.title: 2 · Follow one leaf to its base
steps.look_for: Find where the broad leaf blade joins the wrapping sheath. Notice the rounded, clasping leaf-base shoulders and the pale, hairy-edged ligule (the tiny flap on the inside).
steps.why_it_matters: This close-up is a real Arundo collar with existing arrows. A hairy ligule by itself is NOT enough to separate the reeds.

steps.title: 3 · Look at the top of a flowering cane
steps.look_for: The flower head is a large branching plume made of many slender branches, each carrying tiny spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: A flowering plume is useful, but both Arundo and Phragmites can have feathery heads. Inspect a spikelet next.

steps.title: 4 · See what is inside the plume
steps.look_for: The published photographic plate includes close views of true Arundo spikelets, glumes (the two scales at a spikelet's base) and individual florets (little flowers).
steps.why_it_matters: Arundo's conspicuous silky hairs are mostly associated with the florets/lemmas. Phragmites has long silky hairs along the spikelet axis (rachilla). The exact hair attachment in this plate is not yet verified at microscopic scale.

beginner_learning_path.safety_note: If you only have an unflowered tall reed, use a tentative identification. Don't call it Arundo based on height or plume shape alone; compare the collar and mature reproductive parts.
